summary: The respondent strongly exhibits Public Engagement and Responsiveness dimensions, reflecting the perspective of a disability rights organisation interfacing with municipal infrastructure decisions. Engagement is predominantly framed negatively (polarity N) through accounts of systemic exclusion, where passive public notices replace direct invitations to affected groups. While a meeting occurred following extensive documentation by members, the subsequent lack of substantive action illustrates an obdurate Responsiveness (polarity N), as officials ignored core safety demands and implemented minor peripheral changes months later. Finally, the respondent articulates a positive stance on Public Engagement (polarity P) by demanding upstream inclusion before projects are even conceptualised, asserting that standard consultation is inherently too late.
transcript:
Interview transcript N01 — General secretary, disability rights organisation
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] When did your organisation first hear about this system?
[Respondent] From a member, not from the council. She rang the office because the crossing she uses every day to get to dialysis had changed and she couldn't work out the pattern. That was three weeks after switch-on at her junction. We then found out there had been a consultation event eight months earlier that we hadn't been invited to.
[Interviewer] How did the council explain that?
[Respondent] That it was advertised publicly. Which it was — in the council newsletter and on the website. I've stopped being angry about this particular thing because I've heard it forty times in twenty-six years. Advertising publicly and inviting are different acts. If you want disabled people in the room you write to the six organisations in this city that have disabled members, and there are six, and we all know each other, and it takes an afternoon.
[Interviewer] What did you do once you knew?
[Respondent] What we always do. We collected accounts — we had thirty-one members describing specific junctions within a month, with times and dates, because our members are extremely used to documenting things nobody believes. We put it into a submission with photographs and a map. We asked for a meeting.
[Interviewer] Did you get the meeting?
[Respondent] Yes, after four months. It was a good meeting, I want to say that. Two officers, both engaged, both took notes. And then nothing happened for seven months, and then two crossings got audible confirmation, which was one of nine things we asked for and not one of the top three.
[Interviewer] What were the top three?
[Respondent] Longer minimum crossing intervals as a floor the model cannot go below. A published statement of how the system treats slower pedestrians. And a named person we can contact who has authority to change a junction. Nothing on that list is technically hard. The third one costs nothing at all.
[Interviewer] Has this changed how you approach the next project?
[Respondent] We now ask to be on the distribution list before there is a project. Not for consultations — for the list of things being considered. Consultation is too late by definition. I've said that in every submission I've written for a decade and I'll keep saying it until somebody puts it in a procedure.
